A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across moves.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer experiments on algorithmic tasks and formal languages, plus positional-function fitting experiments in Appendix G.2.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original analyses of trained models' positional products and further APE-versus-NoPE copying experiments in Appendices G.6–G.7.

M1.justification: The proposed Limit Transformer architecture, C-RASP operation set, hypothesis class, regularizer, and idealized inference procedure remain unchanged. The added analyses and theoretical constructions do not introduce a new learning procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix G.7 extends COPY UNIQUE with tasks copying every second or third token; its t-1 task is the existing COPY UNIQUE task. The original algorithmic and formal-language benchmarks remain. The added GPT-2 study examines internal positional products rather than language-modeling benchmark performance.

E2.justification: The original APE, NoPE, and MLP random-baseline comparisons remain. The added copying experiments compare the existing APE and NoPE families; GPT-2 is an object of internal analysis, not an additional competing solution.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings are retained. New Appendix G.7 experiments introduce expanded hyperparameter searches, dropout variation, 5,000-example test sets, and training through length 128 with evaluation through 384. Appendix G.6 introduces offset-variance measurements and attention comparisons across shifted windows.

E4.justification: Appendix G.6 adds extensive checks of approximate translation invariance in five synthetic-task transformers and GPT-2 Small, including individual-head and post-softmax analyses. G.7 tests whether the APE–NoPE distinction persists across copying variants, broader searches, and longer training ranges.

E5.justification: Five-run averaging was already reported in v1 and remains. The added G.7 experiments define successful runs using greater than 99% in-distribution accuracy, versus E.3's retained 100% criterion with a largest-model exception. This changes run inclusion without increasing the reported run count or adding uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Results in Figures 1–6 are retained. New Tables 8–9 report additional copying results: for example, Table 8 gives t-2 accuracy of 0.977 for APE and 0.000 for NoPE at lengths 101–150 after training through 50. Figures 7–11 add findings about approximate translation invariance and exceptional heads. These are additional results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 59 and a construction concerning failure without translation invariance. It revises Lemma 42's morphism-closure argument and corrects C-RASP counting and logical formulas. Theorem 19 drops its separately stated log-precision assumption and expands the precision and communication argument; the main length-generalization theorem is retained.

C1.justification: Both versions claim an idealized asymptotic length-generalization guarantee linked to restricted Limit Transformers, C-RASP expressivity bounds, and empirical prediction of generalization behavior. The rewritten introduction and additional appendix evidence retain these central contributions.

C2.justification: New Appendices G.4 and G.6 explain the APE–NoPE distinction through encoding choices, offset exposure, and bounded-norm positional access. They conjecture that offset-invariant training encourages invariant computations and discuss approximate invariance, boundary effects, and finite-length versus asymptotic behavior. D.3 also adds discussion of replacing Heaviside activations through layer normalization.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies a code-repository link. It also documents the added copying-task generation, search spaces, and selected configurations in Tables 10–11, plus the layer-normalization approximation and token counts used for positional-product analysis. The original implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: G.4 adds a targeted reconciliation with the already cited Kazemnejad work, and G.5 connects the framework to Solomonoff induction. References to Li and Vitanyi, GPT-2, mechanistic interpretability, and the original Transformer are added. The central positioning relative to RASP-L remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction, FAQ, and selected proof explanations are rewritten or expanded, with clearer descriptions of Limit Transformers and new appendix subsections. The established section order and most existing exposition remain; conference headers and bibliography formatting also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 7–11 with variance histograms and positional-product/attention heatmaps, and Tables 8–11 with results and configurations. Existing Figures 1–6 remain, with some figures and tables relocated as the text is reflowed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification of translation invariance, a central assumption that v1 primarily motivates theoretically, by examining trained synthetic-task models and GPT-2 in G.6. The broader copying experiments in G.7 test the APE–NoPE finding more thoroughly. Revised mathematical arguments, detailed configurations, and a code link also improve inspectability and reproducibility. The guarantees remain idealized, and the new invariance evidence is approximate, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.
